en: Regarding the Pure Land, one must seek it from its own primary source;
the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* states: "The Buddha told Maitreya:

'If there are those who hear the name of that Buddha and, with joyful exultation, even for a single thought-moment, take refuge, you should know that such persons have attained great benefit and are fully endowed with the unsurpassed.'"

This is merit. Therefore, Maitreya, even if there were a great fire filling the trichiliocosm, one must pass through it to hear this sutra-dharma, to rejoice with faith and delight, to receive, uphold, read, and recite it, and to practice according to its teaching. Why is this?
There are many bodhisattvas who wish to hear this sutra but are unable to do so. If there are sentient beings who hear this...
As for this Sūtra, one shall never regress from the Unsurpassed Path; therefore, one should single-mindedly believe, accept, uphold, recite, explain, and practice it.
For this purpose, I have given rise to a heart of faith and joy, disregarding slander, and have further compiled this book.

Since you possess the necessary conditions, should there be even a fraction of merit herein, I pray that the Buddha will take pity on me and cause me to go decisively [to the Pure Land] at the time of my death.

May one attain rebirth. May they, by virtue of this merit, swiftly enter the Sahā world and extensively transform sentient beings through the Dharma of this sutra until the end of the future, never wearying.
This is because the grace received in this life from the Pure Land is difficult to repay or requite.
Those who must seek the Pure Land should know that the Pure Land is the adornment of merit; it is profoundly deep and most subtle.
This is the realm [of practice]. One must seek to attain it with a heart that is utterly sincere, earnest, vast, and perfectly harmonious.

Now, this wondrous gateway to the Pure Land is praised by all Buddhas; it is difficult to hear and difficult to know. Thus a sutra says: "There are many bodhisattvas who wish to hear this sutra but are unable to do so.
I am fortunately possessed of the necessary conditions and have already heard and known it; how could I not resolve to [practice it] with certainty?
One must cultivate this mind with speed and realize it. It is like a person who has already ascended a mountain of jewels;

how could they willingly endure suffering and turn back without taking the treasures? Therefore, one should seek them with absolute determination. Every day, recite the name for a fixed number of tens of thousands;
every day, prostrate before the image for a fixed duration, continuing until the end of one's life, facing westward at dawn.
The ten recitations, performed daily before the image with sincere lamentation, must all be undertaken with a resolute will.

If one does not act thus, it is exactly like ascending a mountain of jewels while willingly returning empty-handed; one will continue to transmigrate through the long kalpas as before—is this not tragic?
For this reason, I have specially selected the most essential texts and composed these most urgent admonitions, so that one may achieve final settlement in this single lifetime.
This is the essential scripture. The profound, subtle, and pure realms of the Buddha-lands are all attained from the vast, perfectly interfused, and resolute mind of sentient beings;
therefore, it is titled "The Resolute Seeking of the Pure Land. This is for those of my own kind.
One must read extensively; only then can one give rise to the resolute aspiration and return early to the Pure Land.
Because I have made a vow regarding the precepts, I have accordingly offered forty-eight incense sticks from my own arm as an offering to Amitābha Buddha.
With a sincere heart, he repents and makes this vow: "I now burn my arm as incense to make offering to Amitābha Buddha.
May all my manifold transgressions be definitively extinguished. May I, at the end of my life, be definitively reborn in that land.
May I quickly hear the Buddha Vehicle; may I quickly deliver all beings. By means of these merits, may I adorn the Buddha’s Pure Land and repay the four [debts of gratitude] above."
Deep Gratitude. May those below be rescued from the sufferings of the three miserable realms. Should there be any who see or hear this, may they all resolve to attain Bodhicitta.
Throughout this present life, may we together be reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
Written on the Buddha’s Birthday in the third year of the Guangxu era by the Bhikṣu Yanxi, Yufeng Gukun, at the Ba’en Pass of Fayuan Hermitage, with prostrations.
One must seek the Pure Land;
the method of Buddha-recitation is of profound merit. Be sincere and firm in your resolve, following the words of the Patriarchs. Practice the ten recitations according to the essential commentary;
read the essential commentary to grasp the secret key to holding the name. May you fortunately die with all thoughts of theft extinguished.

Preface to the Four Records on Expressing My Feelings by Invoking the Names [of the Buddhas] upon Being Moved by Anger and Establishing the Practice of Repentance through Reading the Words of the Four Great Patriarchs;
Four Records on Reading Buddhist Verses, along with Questions and Answers;
On the Difficulty of Eliminating Tongue Disease; On Feeling Remorse for Excessive Greed and Anger after Refraining from Eating After Noon; A Vow to Delay Becoming a Master.
1. Self-Repentance for Fondness of Discourse; 2. Carefulness in Speaking of Others’ Faults; 3. Offering Arm Incense for the Brahmajāla Sūtra (Confession);
4. Celebrating the Completion of Seven Days; 5. Expressing One’s Feelings and Informing the Assembly; 6. Walking Meditation During the Six Periods; 7. Chanting the Buddha’s Name Aloud; 8.
Six Verses of Praise Used in the Hall for Reciting the Buddha’s Name.
*Seeking the Pure Land through Devotion to the Great Master [Hui]yuan* (also titled *An Exhortation for the Practice of Pure Karma*).
For students of the practice of pure karma: [May your] minds be forever empty and still;
together, verify that the Dharma-gate of Buddha-recitation is weightier and more sincere.

Those who feel a profound sense of gratitude for the Dharma-gate of the Pure Land truly entered it through the single phrase of "mindfulness of the Buddha" (nianfo) spoken by Master Lianchi at the moment of his death.
Throughout his life, Master Lianchi did not spare his own body or life in propagating the Pure Land teachings;
yet when he reached the time of his passing, seeing the assembly in deep sorrow and earnestly entreating him for further instruction, he could not help but exert his full strength to the end.
The answer is: "Recite the Buddha’s name with sincerity. How great! How inconceivable!
I believe this statement not only encompasses Master T’an-luan’s lifelong teaching of disregarding his own life and body to universally deliver sentient beings;
it truly can encompass Śākyamuni Tathāgata’s forty-nine years of laying bare his heart and liver to universally gather all classes of beings.
Discourse. Why is this so? "Sincerity" (lǎoshí) means ultimate honesty. "Mindfulness" (niàn) refers to the inherently existing spirit and awakening within sentient beings.

"Buddha" is the most supreme fruit among the ten dharma realms. If one invokes that most supreme Buddha with this inherently existing spirit and awakening, then the emotional states of ignorance and darkness, as well as the defiled environments of the nine realms, will immediately become luminous and pure.
"Turbid currents become clear inch by inch when reflected by a pearl; dark chambers are illuminated layer by layer by the light of a precious torch. This is what that means.
That the four lands are perfectly pure and the three bodies are perfectly perceived truly resides herein. Thus, the *Yaojie* states: "A single utterance of 'Namo Amitābha Buddha'..."
This is the Dharma of Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi attained by our original teacher Śākyamuni in this world of five turbidities.
Now, this fruit of awakening is bestowed in its entirety upon sentient beings of this turbid and evil age. This is the realm traversed by all Buddhas;
it can be fully realized only by Buddha after Buddha, and cannot be believed or understood through the self-power of the nine realms.
Therefore, the merit of mindfulness of the Buddha cannot be compared to the noble practices of the Three Vehicles, nor can it be equaled by the blessings and virtues of humans and devas.
Thus, Che-wu said: "If one were to set aside the name of the Buddha and instead cultivate the noble practices of the Three Vehicles..."
This is also a waste of one's spirit and energy; it is like drawing a crossbow capable of launching a thousand-jin bolt to shoot at a mere field mouse.

How much more so when it concerns the creation of karma for the cycle of birth and death within the six realms of existence! I address my fellow practitioners who currently maintain faith and aspiration while reciting the Name: you should feel profound joy.
Were it not for having deeply planted the seeds of Buddhahood and long received the Buddha’s grace, how could you possibly have faith in this Dharma gate? How could you...
One can aspire to this. How could one not exhaust the thieving mind and practice with vigor?
To exhaust the thieving mind means that faith has reached its ultimate limit within a single gate, remaining unassailed by various delusions. It is also what is meant by being "old and honest";
it is also what is meant by reaching the utmost sincerity. One should know that this mind can suddenly transcend the sea of suffering and suddenly enter into bliss.
The state [of rebirth] allows one to see Amitābha instantaneously, and even enables the vast salvation of sentient beings to fulfill the vow of Bodhi.
Thus, the *Amitāyurdhyāna Sūtra* says: "Those who wish to be born in the highest grade of the highest birth must, first of all, give rise to a heart of utmost sincerity.

Therefore, we know that the Tripitaka and the twelve divisions of the scriptures are entirely nothing other than this single phrase of sincere nianfo (recitation of the Buddha's name). I, Kun, write this with the utmost faith in the Lotus [Pure Land].
Master Chih-i was truly an emanation of Amitābha, who came specifically to transmit the secret instructions of this *nien-fo* samādhi.
To encourage those newly entering the path, he further composed a verse, saying:
The sincerity of a straightforward heart is beyond compare; through this practice of nianfo, the Buddha grows ever more pleased. Alas for those of a certain class of clever people:
the more they study the marvelous and extraordinary, the further they stray from the fundamental principle.
Holding the Buddha with a sincere heart, one shall always know the Buddha’s light shining everywhere.
Thus, even those foolish husbands and wives can swiftly escape the prison of the mundane world and enter the jewel pond.
Reciting the Buddha’s name with a sincere heart can cause the pure karma to be swiftly perfected;
therefore, on the day of his passing, our Patriarch Lien (Lianzhu) exhorted people with all his might to follow this practice.
With a sincere heart, diligently recite the Buddha’s name; keep it simple and straightforward, without seeking anything extraordinary.
Because of this, Amitābha will feel even greater compassion and will surely extend his golden arm to receive you early.
Regarding the practice of the ten recitations based on the words of Master Jian:

When Kunchu was first studying under him, he saw renunciants practicing the method of the ten recitations and would always look down upon it, saying, "This is merely something for ordinary laypeople to be taken in by Amitābha Buddha;
because they are busy all day long, they cannot perform many recitations. Thus he spoke.
He made this vow: "If one can practice according to this, one may likewise attain rebirth there. Those who have left the household life have many ritual recitations from morning until evening;
why then must they emphasize these ten recitations? Even a single session of their daily recitations could equal several sets of ten recitations.
This is because they do not understand the essential purpose of the Pure Land school. As for those living as laypeople, they are busy all day long.
Though one may be busy, if one cultivates the ten recitations, the Buddha will certainly embrace and cause one to be reborn in the Pure Land.
How much more so for those who have left the household life, who throughout the day recite various sutras or chant the Buddha’s name many times;

if they can further practice the ten recitations in accordance with the Great Compassionate Vow of Amitābha Buddha, how could Amitābha Buddha not definitely cause such a person to be reborn in the highest grade? Thus it is said.
The Great Patriarchal Master practiced the ten recitations for this very purpose.

At that time, Kun-nan was truly at the height of his folly, disparaging Amitābha Buddha—this Great Compassionate One of Great Vow-Power, the fundamental Dharma-wheel that universally gathers all three capacities of beings.
If it were not for this Dharma, how could those who have committed the ten evils and the five heinous crimes be suddenly gathered and all reborn in the Pure Land?
Therefore, to disparage this Dharma-gate is to disparage the Great Compassionate Vow of Amitābha Buddha.
To disparage the Great Compassionate Vow of Amitābha Buddha is to disparage one's own eternally abiding, indestructible Great Perfect Enlightenment Mind.
Chan Master Chushih recited the ten recitations every morning without fail throughout his life. Master Youxi offered [this practice] daily...
Recitation: never ceasing even unto old age. These two patriarchs were both dragons and elephants of the Dharma; their virtue and realization were complete, known by all far and near.
Yet they still exerted themselves in this way to practice it with all their might. Thus, Great Master Jiānmì said: "This practice of Pure Land cultivation is indispensable.
Even those who recite the Buddha’s name many times should perform it. Kūn pondered these words deeply, when suddenly—
Nevertheless, there was an awakening; I finally realized that the Dharma-gate of the ten recitations is supremely essential and urgent.
Thus, the Venerable Master Ciyun said: "The ten recitations are the most essential cause for purity and must by no means be abandoned. Why is it that intelligent people often refuse to practice them?
It is because they do not know that Amitābha possesses such a great vow, or because their faith is not deep and their aspiration is not urgent. Indeed, if one can...

Practice it. One must have firm faith and vows; thus, one will certainly attain rebirth. Therefore, the *Yaojie* (Essential Explanations) states: "Deep faith and the arousal of vows are themselves unsurpassed bodhi.
This union of faith and vows serves as the definitive guide to the Pure Land. To then uphold the Name based upon this constitutes the primary practice (*samyak-pratipatti*).
If faith and vows are firm, even ten recitations or a single recitation at the moment of death will certainly [lead to rebirth].
Rebirth [in the Pure Land] is possible; even ten recitations at the moment of death can still lead to rebirth, so how much more so for those who practice throughout their entire lives?

How could one not be certain of rebirth? Therefore, on the nineteenth day of the second month in the year of Guihai, I made a vow in the meditation hall of Mount Foding and subsequently exhorted my friends to practice together.
This was recorded in the spring of the Dingchou year at Fayuan Hermitage.
Regarding this point of repaying kindness, he composed a verse, saying:
"The ten recitations suddenly perfect the karma of purity; Amitābha’s compassionate heart was keen during his causal stage. Seeing me suffering, he could not bear to let it cease;
He has specially piloted this vessel to come and welcome me."
Ten recitations instantly perfect the karma of purity; the Cloud of Compassion constantly speaks on behalf of Amitābha. I exhort everyone to always face west at dawn and hold the name;
when their lifespan ends, they will surely be born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.

Ten recitations suddenly perfect the pure karma; even Master Chugong rejoiced. Throughout his life he constantly maintained this mindfulness without ceasing, personally beholding the Buddha’s body pervading and filling all realms.
The ten recitations suddenly perfect the pure karma; the Holy Patriarch Youxi clearly elucidated this. Virtue summons celestial music that frequently descends from the void;
the cultivation of this Dharma shall never be deficient.
(Appendix) The Dharma Gate of the Ten Recitations by Master Cibyun:
Every morning, having dressed and finished one's attire, stand facing west in an upright posture with palms joined. Recite the name of Amitābha Buddha in a continuous voice;

one breath constitutes one recitation. In this manner, ten breaths constitute ten recitations. Follow the natural length of each breath; do not limit the number of recitations to a fixed count of Buddhas.

Counting the breaths as the measure, with the voice neither too high nor too low, neither too slow nor too hurried, maintaining a balanced middle, one connects ten breaths in succession, ensuring the mind does not wander, and making diligent application of effort;
this is called "ten recitations. This is relying on the breath to bind the mind.
Having formed this thought, one makes the vow of dedication, saying:
"I, disciple [Name], single-mindedly take refuge in Amitābha Buddha of the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
May your pure light illuminate me, and may your compassionate vows embrace me. Now, with right mindfulness, I invoke the name of the Tathāgata for the duration of ten recitations."

The path to Bodhi. Seeking rebirth in the Pure Land: according to the Buddha’s original vow, "If there be sentient beings who wish to be born in my land and, with a sincere heart of faith and joy, recite the name even ten times, yet should they not be born there, may I not attain perfect enlightenment—except for those who have committed the five heinous crimes or slandered the true Dharma.
I now recall that since this present life began, I have neither committed such heinous crimes nor slandered the Mahāyāna. I pray...
By these ten recitations, one enters the great ocean of the Tathāgata’s vows. Riding upon the power of the Buddha’s compassion, all transgressions are extinguished and the causes for purity increase.
When approaching the end of life, one will know for oneself that the time has come; the body will not suffer from illness, and the mind will be free from attachment.
The mind will not be inverted or distracted, as if entering meditative concentration. The Buddha and the assembly of sages will come to welcome me, holding golden platforms in their hands.

In the space of a single thought-moment, I shall be born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss; upon the opening of the lotus flower, I shall behold the Buddha, immediately hear the Buddha-vehicle, and suddenly awaken to the Buddha-wisdom.

To extensively deliver sentient beings and fulfill the vows for Bodhi (having performed this, one may cease; it is not necessary to prostrate). One must exhaust this life without allowing even a single day’s temporary abandonment.
By simply ensuring that there is no abandonment, one will personally resolve the mind and be born in the Pure Land.
By reading the *Yaojie*, one can grasp the essential method for upholding the Name.
Whenever I read the section on "Light and Longevity" in the *Wangsheng Lun Yaojie*, I am moved by the utmost gratitude. How fortunate I am to have been able to receive this sublime teaching;
it must surely be the result of the empowerment bestowed by Amitābha Buddha’s two virtues of Light and Longevity. And furthermore—
I am protected and sustained by the great compassionate heart of all Buddhas.

Throughout countless kalpas, the World-Honored Ones of the ten directions and Amitābha Buddha have cultivated the bodhisattva path, not sparing their own bodies or lives, solely for the sake of delivering me; this is its original purpose.
Desiring that this sublime essence may permeate those with whom I share a karmic affinity, I compose these verses:
Simply recite the name while counting on a rosary, and the span of his life and his radiance will fully manifest.
If you wish to accord with the supreme principle of the West, you need only be sincere and cease all discrimination.
Regarding the phrase "merely recollecting the name so that light and lifespan manifest," this should be understood as follows: *Amitābha* is correctly translated as "Immeasurable.
While its essence is fundamentally inexpressible, our Original Teacher [Śākyamuni] encompasses all such immeasurables through the two meanings of light and lifespan.

Light extends horizontally throughout the ten directions, while lifespan reaches vertically to the limits of the three periods of time. When horizontal and vertical dimensions interpenetrate, this is the very substance of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
To take this very essence and manifest it as the body and land of Amitābha is, in fact, to take this very essence and manifest it as the name of Amitābha.

Therefore, the name of Amitābha is precisely the fundamental awakening (hon-gaku) of the rational nature of sentient beings; to hold the name is the union of initial awakening (shiki-gaku) with that fundamental nature.

The beginning and the source are non-dual; the sentient being and the Buddha are non-dual. Therefore, when one thought-moment accords [with reality], one is a Buddha in that very thought-moment; as each thought-moment accords, one is a Buddha in every thought-moment.
Furthermore, by virtue of the meaning of immeasurable light, when sentient beings are born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, they are immediately born throughout the ten directions.
To see Amitābha Buddha is to see all Buddhas of the ten directions. To be able to deliver oneself is to universally [deliver others].
It benefits all beings through the meaning of immeasurable life. Therefore, the people of Sukhāvatī are all those in their final birth before Buddhahood (*ekajātipratibaddha*);
they are all certain to attain Buddhahood in this very life and shall not become ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
One should know that apart from the mind of immeasurable light and life in the present single thought-moment, where could there be the name of Amitābha Buddha? And apart from Amitābha...
By what means can one thoroughly realize the mind of immeasurable light and longevity within this very present thought?
If it is thus, then the ultimate principle resides entirely therein; one need only recite the Buddha’s name with sincerity, without engaging in conceptual discrimination.
Therefore, the *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment* says: "At all times, do not give rise to deluded thoughts. Regarding all deluded minds..."
Nor does it cease; it dwells within the realm of delusive thought, adding no further discernment. Lacking such discernment, one cannot distinguish the reality.
If those sentient beings, upon hearing this Dharma-gate, believe, understand, accept, and uphold it without giving rise to alarm or fear, they are said to be in accord with the nature of awakening.
Such sentient beings have already made offerings to hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Ganges-sands [of Buddhas].

The Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, along with the great Bodhisattvas, have planted the roots of all virtues; the Buddha says that such a person is called one who has accomplished all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvākārajñatā*).

Therefore, Chan Master Che’wu, having attained great enlightenment into Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*),剖心沥血 (cutting open his heart and shedding his blood), praised the recitation of a single Buddha-name, saying:
"If one were to set aside the name of the Buddha and instead practice the holy deeds of the Three Vehicles, it would likewise be a waste."
To employ the spirit is like using a crossbow capable of launching a thousand-jin bolt to strike a mere field mouse; the trigger is pulled for no great purpose.
Great Master Jianmi was the legitimate heir of Lingfeng and attained a profound mastery of the essential meaning. When he invoked the name, it was exhaustive and left nothing unexhausted.

There was no need for the labor of visualization, nor the necessity of investigative inquiry; thus it is said that the single phrase "Amitābha" cannot be realized by anyone who has not attained great penetration.

It is fully present; even the most ignorant lack nothing. Should there be even the slightest bit of conceptual discrimination, it becomes a calamity that brings demonic interference to the Great Dharma.
It is only valued when upheld with single-minded devotion; how could one envy a vague understanding? It is further said:

In this age of the dregs of the kalpa, sentient beings are heavily oppressed by karmic obscurations. Do not mix the practice of *nāmadheya* (reciting the name) with the investigation of *kōan*; do not, with a coarse mind, practice *vipaśyanā* (insight meditation).

If one engages in miscellaneous dialogues with teachers, turbid wisdom will surge like waves and wrong views will arise; in such a state, the practice of superior contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) will not be within one's scope, and demonic obstacles will emerge during meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
One should instead take this very present moment of ignorance—the karmic consciousness of the single thought-moment—and cause it to single-mindedly recite the name of Amitābha Buddha.
If one does so with uninterrupted, focused devotion, there is none who fails to personally realize and personally arrive at [the Pure Land].
This Dharma-gate reaches such a point that the more humble one becomes, the more one cannot look up; the more shallow one becomes, the more one cannot look down.

Self-invocation meets with self-response; self-dreaming meets with self-awakening. The fundamental source of the single mind is suddenly revealed, and the essence and function of the Dharma-realm are fully disclosed.
There is no need for arduous drilling or gazing upward; simply practice in this manner. If you have not yet thoroughly penetrated the root source, how could you possibly—?
Ignorance and the wondrous merge as one. Indeed, for the ignorant and deluded to practice *nianfo* (Buddha-recitation) is ultimate, it is the pinnacle; there is nothing further to add.
This is precisely what is meant by "sincere *nianfo*"—that which does not require analytical discrimination. Such a wondrous practice is inconceivable.
The six directions praise this together, yet even so they cannot exhaust its merit. I pray that all my fellow students will contemplate this deeply, again and again.

I am ashamed that my karmic obstacles from past lives are so profound and heavy that I am unable to propagate such a vast Dharma-gate in this present life to repay the deep kindness of the Buddhas and the Patriarchs.
I can only exert myself with a resolute mind, vowing to dedicate my entire life until death. Sixty thousand *miles*.
I vowed to pay homage and contemplate [the Buddha] during the six periods of the day without fail for even a single day.
At the Baoen Gate of Fayuan Hermitage in Shanyin,
I read the *Yaojie* (Essential Explanations) and fortunately died out my thieving mind.
I, Kun, am deeply ashamed of my heavy defilements. Although I possess the desire to study, I truly lack the resolve to remain dedicated for long.

For this reason, my studies of the Sutras, the Vinaya, Chan, and Pure Land have all failed to reach fruition. Fortunately, upon reading the "Essential Explanation of the Amitābha Sūtra" (Wangsheng lun zhu yaojie), specifically the passage on the five turbidities, I was able to utterly extinguish my thieving mind and focus single-mindedly on holding the Name.
I wish to share this with those of like affinity, that we may together die with our thieving minds extinguished.
Therefore, taking what is most fortunate, he composed this verse:
"Holding the Name is easy; a death-ready mind is difficult. Fortunate indeed to read the *Essential Explanation of Amitābha*.
If you wish to leave the five turbidities for the rest of your life, It will surely be in vain without relying on this practice."
That this practice is not in vain is explained as follows: We dwell within the *kalpa-kāṣāya* (the age of corruption), where we are certainly confined by time and oppressed by suffering;
without a practice that allows for the horizontal transcendence of karmic burdens, we will surely not be able to cross over.

We dwell within the *dṛṣṭi-kāṣāya* (the age of corrupted views), where we are certainly entangled by false wisdom; without a practice that does not rely on skillful means, [we cannot attain liberation].
One will certainly not be able to cross over. Dwelling amidst the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*), one is inevitably swallowed by craving and stung by evil karma;
this is not the practice of the Buddha-mind within the ordinary mind, and thus one will certainly not be able to cross over.
Dwelling amidst the turbidity of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*), one is fixed in foulness and impurity yet lacks penetrating awakening, and remains content in weakness and inferiority.

To soar forth, one must not practice with a mind of attachment and aversion; otherwise, one will certainly be unable to cross over. Dwelling amidst the defilements of life, one is destined to be swallowed by impermanence.
Like a spark from a flint or a flash of lightning, there is no time to prepare. It is not that this does not require vast eons of time nor the diligent practice of arduous toil;
yet without it, one will certainly be unable to cross over. Furthermore, simply through these very elements of faith and aspiration, adorn a single recitation of "Amitābha."
Namu Amida Butsu. By transforming the turbidity of the kalpa into a pure sea assembly; by transforming the turbidity of views into immeasurable light;
by transforming the turbidity of afflictions into the light of eternal tranquility; by transforming the turbidity of sentient beings into birth through transformation within lotus flowers;

and by transforming the turbidity of lifespan into immeasurable life—therefore, one utterance of "Namu Amida Butsu" is the Original Teacher Śākyamuni manifesting amidst the five turbidities of this evil world.
The Dharma of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi attained by the World-Honored One is now bestowed in its entirety, as the fruit of awakening, upon sentient beings of this turbid and evil age.
This is the realm traversed by all Buddhas; only Buddhas can fully exhaust its depths.
It cannot be believed or understood through the self-power of the nine realms. If one does not deeply realize its profound depth...

Difficult! One might suppose there were other methods by which one could emerge from the five turbidities, yet within this burning house, amidst the clamor of frivolous proliferation, only by realizing its extreme difficulty can one finally be willing to exhaust the thieving mind and treasure this single practice.
This is why our Original Teacher spoke of its extreme difficulty with such fervor and deeply exhorted us that we must understand it.

Master Miaoye said: "Although the essential nature of the *nien-fo* samādhi is perfect and complete, one should exhaustively observe the subtle rules and regulations to reform all manner of vulgar faults.
One should harbor great fear even toward minor transgressions; how much more so when I have actually harbored anger toward my fellow practitioners. Let [them]...

The harboring of resentment is a grave transgression. If one does not give rise to great fear and repent with a sincere heart, not only will one fail to attain rebirth [in the Pure Land], but there is also the dread that one will suffer great retribution in future lives. The *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* states:

"If in this life one harbors resentful thoughts and feels even slight malice or jealousy toward others, these feelings will intensify in future lives until they become great enmity. How can one not be afraid? Therefore, in the second year of the Guangxu era...
On the first day of the New Year, he reverently burned nine incense sticks on his arm to seek repentance, composing a verse that said:

"I am ashamed that my defilements are heavy and I frequently give rise to anger; My vexation toward the various worthies is deep and profound. For this reason, I burn nine incense sticks upon my arm, To repent for and eliminate past transgressions, and to train in a mind of loving-kindness.
From now on, I make a vow to take the remainder of my life as my limit; On every first and fifteenth day of the month, I shall certainly do so."
Burn three incense sticks for the arms. With a sincere heart, repent and make this vow: "I now burn incense for my arms as an offering to Amitābha Buddha.
May all my manifold transgressions be definitively extinguished. May I, at the end of my life, be definitively reborn in that land.
May I soon hear the Buddha Vehicle; may I soon deliver all beings. By means of this merit, may I adorn the Buddha’s pure land."
Above, repay the fourfold debt of gratitude; below, relieve the suffering of the three miserable realms. May all who see or hear this give rise to the Bodhicitta.
Throughout this present life, may we together be reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.

I pray only that you, O Great Compassionate One, bear witness to me and accept me into your care."

The fourth seven-day period concluded. Master Chengmiao said in his eulogy: "I trust that during this seventh seven-day period, you will surely rely upon the Buddha’s secret empowerment to achieve samādhi.
I now speak without concealing my own shortcomings, saying to him: "Among the ancients who practiced nianfo, there were many who attained rebirth;
however, how many were those who first attained samādhi and only then attained rebirth? Truly, this requires deep faith and a profound vow."
Indeed, at the time of death, many attain rebirth because they temporarily achieve a state of single-mindedness through the secret empowerment of the Buddha’s power.
Thus, the *Bhadracari-praṇidhāna* states: "When my life is about to end, may all obstacles be completely removed;
may I behold that Buddha Amitābha face-to-face and immediately attain rebirth in the Land of Peace and Bliss. If one first attains the three...
[The interlocutor] said, "What is the use of making vows if one wishes to avoid obstacles at the time of death? Lingfeng replied:

"Whether or not one attains rebirth depends entirely on the presence or absence of faith and aspiration; the high or low level of one’s rank depends entirely on the depth of one’s practice of *nianfo*.

This [text] does not say that one must first achieve a state of single-mindedness without distraction and perfect *samādhi* before being able to attain rebirth; it simply says that one must first achieve single-mindedness."
One who achieves samādhi may indeed attain rebirth in the highest grade of the highest level. You should know that for people of the present age, the defiled mind grows ever more intense;
to first attain single-mindedness without distraction and achieve samādhi—how easy can such a thing be said to be?

For me, merely to seek a will that does not waver has been difficult by the thousands and difficult by the tens of thousands. During these seven periods of retreat, no obstructive conditions have arisen, and I have maintained [the practice].

My mind is at peace; for now, I am able to hear the sound of the Dharma daily, which aids in the arousal of diligence. My faith is ultimate; my vows are ultimate; I exert my full strength in practice.
I feel deep remorse that delusive thoughts are ultimately difficult to extinguish; fortunately, Amitābha’s compassionate vow has gathered me in.
With sincere faith and deep aspiration, one will ultimately attain entry. May all friends with one heart protect the merit of the seven days; this merit shall be inexhaustible and endless.
The merit of the Dharma Master’s lecturing on the sutras to aid the Way is likewise inexhaustible and endless. During these seven weeks, I have been illuminated and benefited;
the grace thus received is also inexhaustible and endless. I vow that in this present life, we shall together be reborn in the Pure Land with certainty.
In the west, we shall together behold Amitābha; until the end of the future, we shall together transform sentient beings.
Seventh: Internally making vows to study the six periods of walking meditation and chanting the Buddha’s name aloud.

Part Five, Section Seven, complete. [Reflecting on] how I have shamelessly let time pass in vain, I suddenly recall that by fortunate chance I have read the Buddhist scriptures, through which I have finally come to know that from beginningless kalpas ago...
They receive the bodies of animals in immeasurable and incalculable numbers; it is likewise for hungry ghosts and those in the hells.
When they are made into mules, they carry loads of a thousand *jin* on their backs while having no food to satisfy their bellies; driven day and night, their suffering is beyond description.

When they are made into oxen, they drag a plow with their shoulders and receive a thousand blows upon their backs; at every step, their pain has no place to be voiced. If they lack strength for even a moment, [they are immediately punished].
To be sent to one's death—how could that not be great suffering? Today, fortunately relying on the power of the Buddha, we have become monks.

Regarding our various enjoyments, we simply desire the freedom to walk in meditation and to chant the Buddha’s name aloud; what suffering could there be in this? Furthermore, we bring joy to all Buddhas and receive the protection of dragons and devas.
We are at peace in the present and shall be reborn in the Pure Land at the end of life. How could such merit and virtue ever be fully measured?
Alas! How can one remain within the "shut-door" practice of nianfo, greedily sitting to nourish the spirit while refusing to open one's mouth?

If one does not attain rebirth in this life, then one’s offerings from the faithful will have been consumed in vain; one will still have to endure the suffering of wearing fur and bearing horns. Thus, Master Sheng'an said:
"If I do not return to the West this time, I shall once again undergo the bitter sufferings of the past. Is this not cause for alarm? This is so.
Therefore, he made this vow before the Buddha: "I, your disciple Gu Kun, reverently burn nine incense sticks from my arm as an offering to Amitābha Buddha.

I pray only that Your Great Compassion may constantly descend upon me, enabling me to recite the Buddha’s name aloud without pain in my chest or head (as I have often experienced slight pain in my chest and head while reciting aloud).
Should there be any karmic obstructions from past lives, I pray You will surely grant me protection; only then shall I be able to exert myself."
Exert yourself against the mind of indolence to perfectly accomplish supreme virtue; may you soon behold Amitābha and extensively deliver all sentient beings.
These six verses of praise for use in the Buddha-Recitation Hall are from the *Essentials of Amitābha*.

May they serve as a compassionate vessel for universal salvation; once they pass through the faculty of hearing, the Way shall not be forgotten, and they shall be proclaimed throughout the six realms of existence.
The protective mindfulness remains long; this is truly the King of Sutras. It leads one to the assembly at the Lotus Pond.
The sutra proclaims the Land of Ultimate Bliss, pure and majestic; the Buddha’s lifespan is boundless, and Amitābha is likewise so. Those who are born there are all noble and virtuous.
The birds and trees discourse on the profound mystery; their sublime excellence surpasses all other explanations.
Joining the assembly at the Lotus Pond, the Name of Amitābha fully manifests his myriad virtues. The merit of upholding it with faith and aspiration is immeasurable, as all Buddhas together extol it.
Boarding this vessel, one reaches the Western Land without wavering; The body becomes golden in hue.

To hold fast to the Name is the wondrous method for escaping suffering. The power of Dharmakara’s vows was strong during his causal stage; In the state of fruition, he emits rays of light from his brow-hair.
Gathering those who are deluded and frantic, we shall go together to the Land of the Nine Lotuses.

There, the Lord of the Fire-House, the King of Great Benevolence, will personally receive us with bodies of golden hue; he will earnestly proclaim that cool purity. There is a Buddha who constantly radiates immeasurable light, and the Wondrous Dharma is being rightly proclaimed.
Celestial music fills the void, resonating day and night. There are immeasurable towers of gold and palaces of jade. If a person upholds [this teaching]...
It is said that those with strong faith and aspiration will certainly go to the other land.
The Buddhas of the six directions extend their broad and long tongues, praising the Western Quarter with one voice: "Those who believe shall be protected and mindful, attaining peace and security;
together they shall return to the field of Ultimate Bliss. How could one dare forget such grace and virtue? One should make firm vows and maintain them throughout the day.
I am called Jingmang (Hurriedly). I must see King Maitreya early.
I shall surely seek the Pure Land.
(End) *The Ten Collections of the Pure Land School* (Appendix).
I am ashamed that my obstacles are deep and my learning shallow; I am not proficient in the written word. Although I have forcefully maintained the Name, my merit is not yet matured.

Furthermore, I am afflicted by illness; how could I possibly respond to inquiries? Therefore, I shall set forth my humble views regarding the titles of the *Ten Collections on the Pure Land School* below, so that those who inquire may easily consult them.
The words are simple but the principles are clear; actual practice is the essential requirement. If one desires [benefit] in this present life...
Rebirth [in the Pure Land] must never be taken lightly. You should know that repaying the Buddha’s kindness lies herein, and likewise, the ruin of one's reputation also lies herein.
Therefore, I lament to myself: for the sake of the Pure Land school, I regret my lack of power. I have compiled these ten writings; my suffering has reached its limit.
How much mental toil have I expended! How much blood have I dried up! How many insults have I incurred! How many setbacks have I endured! Should it be possible...

Having formed a karmic connection with one person, my heart rejoices even after consuming a thousand sorrows. (Master Ciyun said: "If one can exhort a single person to be born in the Pure Land, even if one does not practice oneself, one shall still be reborn in the Buddha-land.
Why do I thus stubbornly show my head? It is entirely because many of my pure friends harbor doubts. Those who believe me should take pity on them.
Recorded with reverence by the monk Yufeng, who was suffering from illness in the summer of Dingchou, longing for the West. Bowing his head.谨识 (Jinshi).

Appendix to "The Ten Pure Lands Must Be Sought":
A Forceful Response to Inquiries.
If there are requests that cannot be fulfilled, respond only by saying: "Every day you must certainly practice the method of ten recitations."
One must certainly recite the Amitābha Sūtra every day. One must certainly chant a certain number of Buddha’s names daily:
for laypeople, starting from one thousand; for monastics, starting from ten thousand, up to many thousands or tens of thousands, each according to their capacity.
This shall continue until the end of life. Possessing this merit, one relies upon the Buddha’s vow to save through ten recitations.
At the moment of death, one will certainly attain rebirth. If even ten recitations lead to rebirth, how much more so a hundred, a thousand, ten thousand, or a million?
To devote one’s entire life to these recitations—how could rebirth not be certain? This is the practice of Guankun himself;
it is a teaching given with utmost earnestness. I pray that those with the karmic affinity will reflect upon it and exert themselves.

I openly confess my past transgressions with profound shame. My cultivation has not been genuine, and my distracted mind is difficult to subdue. While it would have been the right time to exert myself in the practice of *nianfo*, I instead sought to gather here and there in distraction.
Though I repeatedly admonished myself with painful regret, I repeatedly committed the same offenses. Is this not truly a matter of deep lamentation? For this reason...
Furthermore, he lit forty-eight incense sticks and offered them to Amitābha Buddha.

With a sincere heart, he confessed his transgressions to seek repentance, vowing never again to commit offenses that would obstruct his rebirth in the Pure Land. This occurred on the twenty-second day of the sixth month in the year Dingchou.
